claims.text: The relevant high-temperature regime for the proposed mechanism is 0.5–0.7 Tm.
Grain refinement increases the fraction of high-energy grain boundaries.
High-energy grain boundaries accelerate thermally activated boundary diffusion.
Enhanced atomic transport along grain boundaries facilitates grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperature.
Grain-boundary sliding can be the dominant deformation mechanism at high temperature and low strain rate.
At lower temperature and higher strain rate, dislocation slip can replace grain-boundary sliding as the dominant mechanism.
In a refined microstructure, diffusion-driven grain-boundary sliding replaces the dislocation glide dominant in a coarse-grained microstructure.
Diffusion-driven grain-boundary sliding causes an earlier onset of plastic deformation.
Grain-boundary sliding reduces intergranular cohesion and thereby lowers toughness.
Refined specimens will yield earlier than compositionally identical coarse-grained specimens under identical high-temperature testing.
Refined specimens will have lower fracture toughness than the coarse-grained baseline.
Refined specimens will show more prevalent grain-boundary sliding events than coarse-grained specimens.
Dislocation glide remains dominant in the coarse-grained baseline at 0.5–0.7 Tm.
The coarse-grained baseline has relatively higher toughness.
The proposed mechanism applies to tungsten-based and advanced high-temperature steel alloys used in fusion-relevant environments.
Oxidation can influence high-temperature plasticity and the quantitative mechanical response.
A same-composition refined-versus-coarse comparison under identical temperature and strain-rate conditions is the proposed control for testing the grain-boundary hypothesis.
Failure to observe earlier plasticity, reduced toughness, or increased grain-boundary sliding in the refined specimens would falsify the proposed mechanism.
